Aim and objectives

Aim. To build the foundations of evidence-based practice for MRCPsych Paper B: where evidence comes from, how to ask and search for it, and how guidelines turn it into shared decisions.

At the end of this workbook, you should be able to:

  1. Describe the hierarchy of evidence and explain why systematic reviews of RCTs sit above observational studies and expert opinion.
  2. Apply the five steps of evidence-based practice and frame a clinical question using PECO(t).
  3. Describe how to search electronic databases completely, using Boolean operators, MeSH terms and multiple databases.
  4. Explain how NICE guidelines are developed, their strengths and limits, and why declarations of interest and funding matter.
  5. Name the main reporting guidelines (CONSORT, STROBE, PRISMA, STARD) and the study design each covers.
  6. Complete all 30 worked challenges, scoring at least 24 (80%), before you open the working.
  7. Answer every quick-recall card out loud, getting at least 80% right, by the end of today's session.

Part 1 · Core ideas

Category 113.1, 13.2.4 · Evidence, clinical questions and causation

13.1.2Evidence hierarchy and sources

Big idea. The best evidence is whichever design best answers the question in front of you, found by a search that someone else could repeat.
Picture it as a library where each shelf answers a different question.

Syllabus: Appraising by design, sources and hierarchy of evidence, electronic databases and cataloguing research for retrieval

Read more in your textbookResearch Methods, page 12 · Sources of evidence and databases →

The story in plain words. Imagine a guideline group with a simple question: does cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia help people with depression sleep? One trial says yes, another no. The hierarchy of evidence tells them where to look first: a systematic review of randomised trials, then single trials, then cohort and case-control studies, then case series, and at the foot expert opinion and reasoning from mechanism. That ladder is built for treatment questions. Change the question and the top rung moves. Prognosis is best answered by an inception cohort gathered at first presentation. A rare harm, such as a skin reaction in 1 in 10,000 users, is best chased by a case-control study that starts with the cases. A rare exposure calls for a cohort chosen on exposure, and a diagnostic question needs a cross-sectional comparison against a reference standard. ((? Why not run a randomised trial to learn how anorexia nervosa unfolds over ten years? ?)) Nobody can be randomised to an illness, and the question is about natural course, so a cohort recruited at the start of illness is the right tool. A clinic sample would overweight the chronic cases.

The people and the evidence. Sackett and colleagues (1996) defined evidence-based medicine as integrating individual clinical expertise with the best available external evidence, with the patient's rights and preferences in view. The Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (2011) then made the question-first idea formal: its levels table has separate rows for treatment, prognosis, diagnosis and harm, each with a different design at level 1. Finding the evidence is its own skill. MEDLINE is the core biomedical index and PubMed is its free front door, which also holds a few newer records not yet indexed; it is not a separate evidence base. Embase adds European and drug journals, PsycINFO psychology, CINAHL nursing and allied health, and Cochrane CENTRAL registers controlled trials. The Cochrane Handbook expects several databases, because no single one covers everything.

From everyday life to the clinic. A search works like a fishing net. Synonyms joined with OR widen the catch to every way of saying the same thing; concepts joined with AND narrow it to papers that contain both. MeSH headings are the indexers' own labels, so one heading gathers papers that say major depression, unipolar depression or MDD. Truncation with * catches word endings, so schizophren* finds schizophrenia and schizophreniform, while a stem as short as psych* drowns you in noise. Good strategies pair MeSH with free text, because the newest papers are not yet indexed. Appraisal then starts with design: for a case-control study, ask first whether cases and controls came from the same source population.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The commonest trap is a stem about prognosis or rare harm that tempts you towards a randomised trial because it sits near the top of the familiar pyramid. Ask what kind of question it is before you choose the rung. The second is databases: PubMed is a free door into MEDLINE rather than a separate evidence base, CINAHL is for nursing, and joining synonyms with AND shrinks a search rather than broadening it. The third is ranking a consensus of eminent experts above a carefully observed case series. Opinion is the foundation, not the roof.

Sources
  1. Richardson WS, Wilson MC, Nishikawa J, Hayward RS (1995). The well-built clinical question: a key to evidence-based decisions. ACP J Club, 123: A12-A13.
  2. Stacey D, Legare F, Lewis K et al (2017). Decision aids for people facing health treatment or screening decisions. Cochrane Database Syst Rev, 4: CD001431.
  3. Hill AB (1965). The environment and disease: association or causation? Proc R Soc Med, 58: 295-300.
  4. Greenland S, Pearl J, Robins JM (1999). Causal diagrams for epidemiologic research. Epidemiology, 10: 37-48.

13.1.5Clinical questions and shared decisions

Big idea. A sharp question picks the study you need, and an honest number, given as people out of a hundred, lets the patient decide what it means for her.
Picture it as a shopping list before the supermarket.

Syllabus: Formulating clinical questions using population, exposure or intervention, comparison, outcome and time, and strategies for enabling the patient to make an informed decision

Read more in your textbookResearch Methods, page 19 · Framing clinical questions: PICO →

The story in plain words. Walk into a supermarket without a list and you leave with biscuits and no bread. A clinical question without structure does the same to a search. PICO names the Population, the Intervention, the Comparison and the Outcome, and adding T pins down the time frame. For a question about harm or cause, the intervention becomes an exposure, so the frame is PECOT. In adults over 65 started on an SSRI, compared with similar adults not on an antidepressant, is hyponatraemia more common within 30 days? Each element turns into search terms, and the shape of the question tells you the design: here a cohort. ((? In that question, what is the C? ?)) Similar adults not prescribed an antidepressant. The comparison is always the group the exposed are measured against, never the exposure itself. The time element matters too, because SSRI hyponatraemia clusters in the first weeks, and a study with five years of follow-up answers a different question.

The people and the evidence. Richardson and colleagues (1995) described the well-built clinical question in the ACP Journal Club, and the four-part frame has shaped evidence-based teaching ever since. Gigerenzer and colleagues (2007) showed that doctors and patients alike misread relative risks and conditional probabilities, but understand natural frequencies: 20 out of 100 people. Stacey and colleagues (2017), pooling more than 100 trials of decision aids, found that people became better informed, more accurate about risk and less conflicted about their choice. The aids are designed to inform rather than steer; the main shift in choices was that fewer people opted for major elective surgery.

From everyday life to the clinic. A woman with recurrent depression asks whether to continue her antidepressant. Over a year, 40 in 100 people like her relapse after stopping and 20 in 100 on continuation. That is an absolute risk reduction of 20 in 100, so 5 people need to continue for one to stay well who otherwise would not. 'It halves your risk' is also true, and tells her far less. NICE guideline NG197 (2021) asks clinicians to use absolute risks with one denominator, to give benefits and harms over the same period, and to check understanding, for example with teach-back: the patient explains the plan in her own words. Asking 'do you understand?' and accepting yes is not a check.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Stems often name the exposure and then ask for the comparison. The answer is the unexposed group or the alternative treatment, not the exposure and not the outcome. A phrase such as 'within 30 days' is the T. In risk communication questions the trap answer quotes only the relative risk reduction, or uses different denominators for benefit and harm. Pick the option that gives absolute numbers as people out of a hundred over a stated time. Decision aids inform; they do not exist to raise uptake of a favoured treatment.

Sources
  1. Rothman KJ (1976). Causes. Am J Epidemiol, 104: 587-592.
  2. Greenhalgh T (2019). How to Read a Paper: The Basics of Evidence-Based Healthcare, 6th ed. Wiley-Blackwell.
  3. Straus SE, Glasziou P, Richardson WS, Haynes RB (2019). Evidence-Based Medicine: How to Practice and Teach EBM, 5th ed. Elsevier.
  4. OCEBM Levels of Evidence Working Group (2011). The Oxford 2011 Levels of Evidence. Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine.

13.2.4Arguing cause and effect

Big idea. An association becomes a cause only when the timing is right and the other explanations have been argued away, and no single checklist does that for you.
Picture it as a detective building a case rather than waiting for a confession.

Syllabus: Approaches for arguing a cause-and-effect relationship: experimental and observational designs, Bradford Hill, Koch, Rothman, Susser and other causation theories

Read more in your textbookResearch Methods, page 25 · Cause and effect: Bradford Hill →

The story in plain words. Austin Bradford Hill gave a lecture in 1965 that still frames the argument. He offered nine viewpoints: strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment and analogy. He was clear they were aids to judgement, not a checklist to score. Only one is essential. A cause must come before its effect, so temporality cannot be missing, and a cohort that records exposure before the outcome shows it better than a case-control study that asks afterwards. Specificity is the weakest, because childhood adversity raises the risk of depression, psychosis and substance misuse alike. Sensitivity is not on the list at all. Rothman (1976) pictured causes as pies. Each whole pie is a sufficient cause, each slice a component cause, and a slice found in every pie is a necessary cause. ((? Genetic liability, cannabis and childhood adversity complete one pie. What is that pie? ?)) A sufficient cause, which is why most cannabis users never develop psychosis: they lack the other slices.

The people and the evidence. Hill's viewpoints grew out of the smoking story. Doll and Hill (1950) found that people with lung cancer were far more often heavy smokers, and the gradient, consistency and timing that followed built the case. Psychiatry has its own experiment example: when British domestic gas was detoxified in the 1960s and early 1970s, suicide by gas almost vanished and the overall rate fell with it, as Kreitman (1976) showed. Finding no dose-response does not refute a cause. A threshold, a plateau, a narrow range of exposure or crude measurement can hide a real gradient. When the rest of the evidence is strong, the least likely explanation is that the exposure does nothing at all.

From everyday life to the clinic. Koch's postulates were written for tuberculosis: one organism, found in every case, grown alone and reproducing the disease. Evans (1976) showed why they fail for complex disorders, and schizophrenia has no single agent that is necessary and sufficient. Susser (1991) reduced the essentials to three: association, time order and direction. Modern causal inference asks a counterfactual question: would the outcome have differed had these same people not been exposed? We never see both versions, so a comparison group stands in, and randomisation makes it a fair stand-in. A directed acyclic graph makes the assumptions visible: adjust for a confounder such as childhood trauma, but not for a mediator or a collider.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The classic distractor in 'which is NOT a Hill criterion' is sensitivity, borrowed from test accuracy. Specificity is on the list and is the weakest; temporality is the only essential one. Keep the models apart. A slice in every pie is necessary and a complete pie is sufficient. Susser's three essentials are association, time order and direction. An experiment is defined by the investigator assigning the exposure, not by being prospective.

Sources
  1. Kreitman N (1976). The coal gas story: United Kingdom suicide rates, 1960-71. Br J Prev Soc Med, 30: 86-93.
  2. Sackett DL, Rosenberg WMC, Gray JAM, Haynes RB, Richardson WS (1996). Evidence based medicine: what it is and what it isn't. BMJ, 312: 71-72.
  3. Evans AS (1976). Causation and disease: the Henle-Koch postulates revisited. Yale J Biol Med, 49: 175-195.
  4. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2021). Shared decision making. NICE guideline NG197.
  5. Gigerenzer G, Gaissmaier W, Kurz-Milcke E, Schwartz LM, Woloshin S (2007). Helping doctors and patients make sense of health statistics. Psychol Sci Public Interest, 8: 53-96.
  6. Higgins JPT, Thomas J, Chandler J et al (eds) (2024). Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, version 6.5. Cochrane.
  7. Grimes DA, Schulz KF (2002). An overview of clinical research: the lay of the land. Lancet, 359: 57-61.

Category 213.9 · EBM principles, evidence sources and guidelines

13.1.2Sources and the hierarchy of evidence

Big idea. The hierarchy ranks study designs by how well they protect a treatment answer from bias, so it tells you which evidence to trust first, not which evidence to ignore.
Picture it as a ladder where each rung removes one more way of fooling yourself.

Syllabus: Different sources and hierarchy of evidence

The story in plain words. Imagine deciding whether a new route to work is faster. One colleague swears it is (expert opinion). A few people tried it once (case series). Someone compared drivers who chose it with drivers who did not (cohort). Best of all, a coin decided who drove which way on the same mornings (randomised trial), and best again, every such coin-toss experiment was gathered and combined (systematic review with meta-analysis). Each rung up the ladder removes a way of fooling yourself. Randomisation removes the choice that lets keen drivers pick the new route. Pooling many trials removes the luck of one small sample. That is why a systematic review of good randomised trials sits at the top for questions about treatment. ((? A review pools two randomised trials with nine uncontrolled studies. Is pooling forbidden? ?)) No. It is possible, but the mix of designs weakens the result, and analysing the trials separately is wiser.

The hierarchy of evidence for a treatment question. Each step up closes off another source of bias. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. Archie Cochrane argued in 1972 that the NHS should be judged by randomised evidence, and the review collaboration later took his name. Gordon Guyatt at McMaster coined the term evidence-based medicine in 1991, his working group launched it in JAMA in 1992, and David Sackett defined it in 1996 as the conscientious use of current best evidence, integrated with clinical expertise and the patient's values. The Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine tables make the point that the best design depends on the question. Prognosis is best answered by inception cohorts and diagnosis by cross-sectional comparison with a reference standard. In practice, rare harms are often first detected by case-control studies and surveillance, because trials are too small to see them.

From everyday life to the clinic. In clinic, a trainee reads a striking case series of ketamine responders and a later systematic review of randomised trials that is more cautious. The review wins, not because case series are worthless, but because it was built to resist bias. Journal reputation is a different scale altogether. The impact factor is the average number of citations to a journal's recent articles. It describes the journal, varies widely by subject area, and says nothing about whether one particular paper is sound.

Everyday picture: a ladder. Each rung removes one more way of fooling yourself. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Expect a question that orders designs from strongest to weakest: systematic review of RCTs, RCT, cohort, case-control, case series, expert opinion. Watch for distractors that put a single trial above a review, or a meta-analysis of observational studies above a good RCT. Expect also the impact factor trap. It rates the journal, never the individual article or author, and it is not a step in appraising a paper.

Exam trap: the order to remember, and the classic wrong moves. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Page MJ, McKenzie JE, Bossuyt PM et al. (2021). The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. BMJ, 372: n71.
  2. Dalkey N, Helmer O (1963). An experimental application of the Delphi method to the use of experts. Management Science, 9: 458-467.
  3. Schulz KF, Altman DG, Moher D, for the CONSORT Group (2010). CONSORT 2010 Statement: updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomised trials. BMJ, 340: c332.
  4. Garfield E (2006). The history and meaning of the journal impact factor. JAMA, 295: 90-93.
  5. Gigerenzer G, Gaissmaier W, Kurz-Milcke E et al. (2007). Helping doctors and patients make sense of health statistics. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 8: 53-96.

13.1.3Electronic databases and complete searching

Big idea. No single database holds all the evidence, so a complete search uses several databases plus trial registries and grey literature to catch the studies that journals never printed.
Picture it as fishing several lakes, then checking the nets nobody hauled in.

Syllabus: Difference between various electronic databases

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 43 · Systematic reviews and meta-analysis →Research Methods, page 12 · Sources of evidence and databases →

The story in plain words. Think of the evidence as fish spread across several lakes. MEDLINE, searched free through PubMed, is the big general lake of biomedical journals. Embase overlaps it but holds more drug and European journals. PsycINFO holds psychology, including literature going back over a century. CINAHL holds nursing and allied health, such as occupational therapy. The Cochrane Library is different in kind: it holds finished systematic reviews and CENTRAL, a register of controlled trials. Even so, it does not contain every trial ever run. Some fish never reach any lake. Trials that were never published, or are still running, are found in trial registries such as ClinicalTrials.gov and ISRCTN. Theses, conference abstracts and reports form the grey literature. ((? Why does leaving out grey literature matter? ?)) Unpublished studies are more often negative, so ignoring them inflates the apparent effect.

What each source holds. Journal databases overlap; registries and grey literature sit outside them. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. In 2004 the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors announced that its journals would only publish trials registered before the first patient was enrolled. Registration made it far harder for a disappointing trial to vanish. Hopewell and colleagues showed in a Cochrane methodology review that trials found only in the grey literature tend to show smaller effects than published ones, so leaving them out pushes results in a favourable direction.

From everyday life to the clinic. A team reviewing psychological therapy for body dysmorphic disorder searches MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO, checks reference lists, writes to experts, searches registries and accepts any language. Each step catches studies the others miss. A pharmacist asking whether trials of a new long-acting antipsychotic are under way, or were finished but never published, goes straight to a registry, because a journal database can only show what was printed. Bramer and colleagues found in 2017 that no single database retrieved every relevant study for the reviews they tested; combining Embase, MEDLINE, Web of Science and Google Scholar was needed to reach near-complete recall.

Everyday picture: fishing several overlapping lakes. One net in one lake misses fish, and some fish never reach a lake. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Match the need to the source: nursing or allied practice to CINAHL, historical psychology to PsycINFO, reviews to Cochrane, ongoing or unpublished trials to a registry, national recommendations to NICE or SIGN. The classic wrong answer is that a good search should exclude conference abstracts or unpublished work because it was not peer reviewed. That is the step that most threatens completeness.

Exam trap: match the question to the source, and do not pick the classic wrong answer. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Cochrane AL (1972). Effectiveness and Efficiency: Random Reflections on Health Services. Nuffield Provincial Hospitals Trust.
  2. Hopewell S, Chan AW, Collins GS et al. (2025). CONSORT 2025 statement: updated guideline for reporting randomised trials. BMJ, 389: e081123.
  3. Elwyn G, Frosch D, Thomson R et al. (2012). Shared decision making: a model for clinical practice. Journal of General Internal Medicine, 27: 1361-1367.
  4. Husereau D, Drummond M, Augustovski F et al. (2022). Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards 2022 (CHEERS 2022) statement. BMJ, 376: e067975.

13.1.5Asking an answerable question: the five steps and PECO(t)

Big idea. Evidence-based practice starts with a sharp question, and PECO(t) sharpens it by naming the people, the exposure or treatment, the comparison, the outcome and the time frame.
Picture it as writing a shopping list before you enter the supermarket.

Syllabus: Formulating clinical questions using the patient exposure or intervention, comparison, outcome, time (PECO(t)) formula

The story in plain words. Walk into a supermarket without a list and you leave with the wrong things. A vague clinical question works the same way. The five steps of evidence-based practice are: ask an answerable question, acquire the best evidence, appraise it, apply it with the patient's values and your expertise, and assess how it went. The shopping list is PECO(t): Population, Exposure (or Intervention, which is why the same frame is often called PICO), Comparison, Outcome and time. 'Does exercise help depression?' becomes: in adults with moderate depression, does supervised exercise, compared with usual care alone, increase remission at 12 weeks? ((? In PECO, what does the E stand for? ?)) Exposure, used for questions about causes and harms, where nobody is assigned a treatment.

The five steps of evidence-based practice and a worked PECO(t) frame. Checking an impact factor is not a step. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. Richardson, Wilson, Nishikawa and Hayward described the well-built clinical question in 1995, showing that naming each part turns a vague worry into search terms. Straus, Glasziou, Richardson and Haynes built the five steps into the standard teaching text. Frames can be adapted: PICOT adds time, PECO suits aetiology, and qualitative questions use other frames, but the principle is the same.

From everyday life to the clinic. A woman with obsessive-compulsive disorder asks how likely sertraline is to cause weight gain. The intervention is sertraline; the outcome is weight gain; the population is people with obsessive-compulsive disorder. The comparison is what she would otherwise do, which is usually no treatment, not a different drug. Choosing that comparator gives her the number that matters to her decision: how much extra risk the tablet adds over not taking it. The time element earns its place too. Weight gain after 8 weeks and after 2 years are different questions with different answers, and a search that ignores time may return the wrong studies.

Everyday picture: a shopping list written before the supermarket, so the search brings back the right things. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The commonest trap is a step that sounds scholarly but is not in the cycle, such as checking the journal's impact factor or the author's seniority. The second trap is the comparator. For a side-effect question the honest comparison is usually people with the same disorder who are not taking the drug, not healthy people and not people on an alternative. A third trap swaps the letters: PECO is the aetiology version, so a stem about an exposure such as cannabis use expects E, while a stem about a treatment expects I.

Exam trap: the comparator for a side-effect question is the same population without the drug. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. von Elm E, Altman DG, Egger M et al. (2007). The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement: guidelines for reporting observational studies. Lancet, 370: 1453-1457.
  2. Sackett DL, Rosenberg WMC, Gray JAM, Haynes RB, Richardson WS (1996). Evidence based medicine: what it is and what it isn't. BMJ, 312: 71-72.

13.1.7Helping the patient make an informed decision

Big idea. Patients decide best when benefit and harm are given as absolute numbers in natural frequencies, so the number needed to treat usually tells them more than a relative risk reduction.
Picture it as showing a hundred faces instead of quoting a percentage.

Syllabus: Strategies for enabling the patient to make an informed decision

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 29 · Communicating risk and shared decisions →

The story in plain words. Tell someone a treatment halves their risk and it sounds dramatic. Show them a hundred faces instead. Without maintenance treatment, 40 of 100 relapse in a year; with it, 20 do. The relative risk reduction is 50%, the absolute risk reduction is 20 percentage points, and the number needed to treat is 1 / 0.20 = 5. The same 50% relative reduction applied to someone whose risk is only 4% saves just 2 relapses per hundred, a number needed to treat of 50. Relative figures hide the patient's starting risk; absolute figures do not. ((? Which single measure best explains benefit to a patient? ?)) The number needed to treat, ideally with the absolute risks and the number needed to harm beside it.

An icon array: the same trial shown as people. Relative risk reduction 50%, absolute risk reduction 20 points, number needed to treat 5. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. Laupacis, Sackett and Roberts introduced the number needed to treat in 1988 as a clinically useful measure. Gigerenzer and colleagues showed that both doctors and patients misread relative risks and conditional probabilities, and understand natural frequencies and pictures far better. Elwyn and colleagues set out a model for shared decision making in 2012: introduce the choice, describe the options with their benefits and harms, then help the person decide what matters most to them.

From everyday life to the clinic. A man with recurrent depression asks how much difference maintenance treatment would make. You show him that about one person in five avoids a relapse they would otherwise have had, then set that against the side-effects he is worried about. Decision aids, icon arrays and a frank account of uncertainty all help. So does checking back: ask him to say in his own words what the numbers mean for him.

Everyday picture: five people like him take maintenance treatment for a year; one avoids a relapse he would otherwise have had. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Distractors include the odds ratio, the control event rate and the relative risk reduction alone. None of them, on their own, tells a patient how many people like him benefit. Remember the direction of the arithmetic: the number needed to treat is 1 / ARR, never 1 / RRR. Finally, the number needed to treat always belongs to a time frame and a comparison. Five people treated for a year against placebo is not the same claim as five people treated for a month against another drug.

Exam trap: the same relative reduction gives very different absolute benefit at different baseline risks. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Greenhalgh T (2019). How to Read a Paper: The Basics of Evidence-Based Medicine and Healthcare, 6th ed. Wiley-Blackwell.
  2. Lexchin J, Bero LA, Djulbegovic B, Clark O (2003). Pharmaceutical industry sponsorship and research outcome and quality: systematic review. BMJ, 326: 1167-1170.
  3. Evidence-Based Medicine Working Group (1992). Evidence-based medicine: a new approach to teaching the practice of medicine. JAMA, 268: 2420-2425.

13.12.1Reporting guidelines

Big idea. Each study design has its own reporting checklist, and the exam tests whether you can match the design to the statement and know that PRISMA has replaced QUOROM.
Picture it as a recipe card that tells the reader exactly what went into the dish.

Syllabus: Guidelines: CONSORT, QUOROM, STARD, PRISMA and SRQR

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 124 · Reporting guidelines: CONSORT, STARD, PRISMA →

The story in plain words. A recipe card lets a cook check whether a dish was made properly. A reporting guideline does the same for a paper: it lists what must be written down so a reader can judge the study and repeat it. The design decides the card. Randomised trials use CONSORT, with its participant flow diagram. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses use PRISMA. Diagnostic accuracy studies use STARD. Cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies use STROBE. Qualitative studies use SRQR or COREQ, and economic evaluations use CHEERS. ((? Which statement should authors of a new meta-analysis follow? ?)) PRISMA. Its predecessor for meta-analyses of trials, QUOROM, was replaced in 2009.

Choose the reporting statement from what the study did. QUOROM (1999) was superseded by PRISMA in 2009. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. Moher and colleagues published QUOROM in 1999. It became PRISMA in 2009 and PRISMA 2020 updated it. CONSORT first appeared in 1996 and was revised in 2001, 2010 and 2025. STARD dates from 2003, updated 2015; STROBE from 2007; SRQR from 2014. These checklists improve reporting; they are not tools for scoring a study's quality.

From everyday life to the clinic. When you appraise a review of lithium for suicide prevention, the PRISMA flow diagram shows how many records were found, screened, excluded with reasons and finally included. A missing flow diagram is a warning sign. Peer reviewers often ask authors to attach the completed checklist, so the items can be found page by page. For a trial, the CONSORT diagram is the first place to look: it shows how many people were assessed, randomised, lost to follow-up and analysed in each arm. If the numbers do not add up, or losses have no reasons, the conclusions deserve less trust. The EQUATOR Network keeps a library of these statements, so for an unusual design, such as a case report or a quality improvement study, there is usually a checklist to find.

Everyday picture: a recipe card lists what went into the dish; a reporting checklist lists what went into the study. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Do not pick QUOROM as the current standard for a systematic review, and do not confuse reporting statements with bodies such as NICE or with databases such as Embase. Match carefully: observational designs to STROBE, accuracy to STARD, trials to CONSORT, reviews to PRISMA.

Exam trap: match design to statement, and remember that checklists guide reporting rather than score quality. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Richardson WS, Wilson MC, Nishikawa J, Hayward RS (1995). The well-built clinical question: a key to evidence-based decisions. ACP Journal Club, 123: A12-13.
  2. Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (2019). SIGN 50: a guideline developer's handbook. SIGN.
  3. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2014, updated 2024). Developing NICE guidelines: the manual (PMG20). NICE.
  4. Hopewell S, McDonald S, Clarke M, Egger M (2007). Grey literature in meta-analyses of randomized trials of health care interventions. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MR000010.
  5. Bramer WM, Rethlefsen ML, Kleijnen J, Franco OH (2017). Optimal database combinations for literature searches in systematic reviews: a prospective exploratory study. Systematic Reviews, 6: 245.
  6. Woolf SH, Grol R, Hutchinson A, Eccles M, Grimshaw J (1999). Potential benefits, limitations, and harms of clinical guidelines. BMJ, 318: 527-530.
  7. OCEBM Levels of Evidence Working Group (2011). The Oxford 2011 Levels of Evidence. Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine.
  8. International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (2024). Recommendations for the Conduct, Reporting, Editing, and Publication of Scholarly Work in Medical Journals. ICMJE.

13.12.2How national guidelines are made

Big idea. A sound guideline is built on a systematic search and appraisal of the evidence, then a committee turns that evidence into recommendations by weighing benefits, harms, costs, values and resources in the open.
Picture it as an architect who surveys the ground before drawing the house.

Syllabus: Process for developing national guidelines, such as NICE and SIGN guidelines

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 130 · Reporting guidelines: CONSORT, STARD, PRISMA →

The story in plain words. An architect surveys the ground before drawing a house. A guideline panel does the same: it scopes the topic, writes review questions in PICO form, and then runs a systematic search for all the evidence. Everything later stands on that survey. The evidence is appraised and graded, then a committee of clinicians, patients and carers weighs it alongside harms, costs and the resources available. Drafts go out for public consultation before publication, and the guideline is kept under surveillance and updated. ((? Where evidence is thin, how can a panel still agree a recommendation? ?)) By formal consensus such as the Delphi method: anonymous rating over several rounds, with the group's results fed back between rounds.

Stages in building a national guideline. The systematic search is the foundation; formal consensus is used only where evidence is thin. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. NICE produces guidance for England and SIGN, the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network, for Scotland. Both draw on the GRADE approach, published by Guyatt and colleagues in 2008, which separates the certainty of evidence from the strength of a recommendation. The Delphi method was developed at the RAND Corporation and described by Dalkey and Helmer in 1963; Hasson and colleagues later set out research guidelines for using it in health.

From everyday life to the clinic. A panel drafting a guideline on treatment-resistant schizophrenia invites stakeholders, but its recommendations are only as good as its search and appraisal. Expert enthusiasm cannot replace a missing trial. Resources are part of the process, not an afterthought. Recommending depot clinics in an area without them helps nobody unless the guideline also says how to provide them. Patients and carers sit on the committee for a reason. They know which outcomes matter in daily life, such as being able to work, sleep and keep a tenancy, and their presence keeps the recommendations tied to those outcomes.

Everyday picture: a house. The systematic review is the foundation on which every recommendation stands. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The most important single foundation is the systematic review of evidence, not consulting every stakeholder or running a fresh meta-analysis for every question. A recommendation written without regard to local resources is the odd one out in a list of sound steps. Delphi is a consensus technique, not a meta-analysis or a survival plot.

Exam trap: the foundation of a guideline, and the distractors that sound important but are not. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. O'Brien BC, Harris IB, Beckman TJ, Reed DA, Cook DA (2014). Standards for reporting qualitative research: a synthesis of recommendations. Academic Medicine, 89: 1245-1251.
  2. Shojania KG, Jennings A, Mayhew A et al. (2009). The effects of on-screen, point of care computer reminders on processes and outcomes of care. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, CD001096.
  3. Hasson F, Keeney S, McKenna H (2000). Research guidelines for the Delphi survey technique. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 32: 1008-1015.
  4. De Angelis C, Drazen JM, Frizelle FA et al. (2004). Clinical trial registration: a statement from the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors. NEJM, 351: 1250-1251.
  5. Higgins JPT, Thomas J, Chandler J et al. (eds) (2023). Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, version 6.4. Cochrane.

13.12.3Strengths, limits and implementation of guidelines

Big idea. Guidelines reduce unwarranted variation, but they reflect values and resources as well as evidence, and they only change care when they are delivered at the moment of decision.
Picture it as a satnav: it helps most when it speaks at the junction, not when the map is posted to you.

Syllabus: Advantages and limitations of guidelines and protocols

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 130 · Reporting guidelines: CONSORT, STARD, PRISMA →

The story in plain words. A satnav is most useful when it speaks at the junction. Posting someone a printed map changes little. Guidelines behave the same way: passive dissemination, such as posting copies or sending a circular, rarely changes what clinicians do. Strategies that reach the clinician at the moment of decision work better. A patient-specific reminder in the electronic record, prompting physical health checks for someone on an antipsychotic, is among the most consistently effective single tactics, although even reminders improve care only modestly. Educational outreach and audit with feedback also help. ((? Why might two countries reading the same trials recommend different things? ?)) Because guidelines also weigh costs, resources and values, which differ between health systems.

Implementation strategies ordered by how active they are and how close they come to the clinical decision. The order is conceptual, drawn from reviews showing passive dissemination has least effect. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. Woolf and colleagues set out in 1999 the potential benefits, limits and harms of guidelines: more consistent care and support for patients' choices, but also the risk of outdated, biased or inflexible advice that ignores the individual. Grimshaw and colleagues reviewed 235 studies of implementation strategies in 2004 and found mostly modest effects, with reminders among the more consistently effective. Shojania and colleagues later showed that on-screen point-of-care reminders improved care by a median of about 4 percentage points.

From everyday life to the clinic. A woman with mild Alzheimer's disease may be eligible for a drug under one country's guideline and not another's. The trials are the same; the cost thresholds and priorities are not. In the clinic a guideline is a starting point. A clinician may depart from it for a good reason and should record why. A ward that wants better lithium monitoring might combine methods: an alert in the record when a level is due, a short teaching session for the team, and a quarterly audit fed back to the prescribers. Layering active methods works better than any one poster. Protocols are stricter than guidelines. A protocol sets out exactly what to do in a defined situation, such as rapid tranquillisation, and leaves less room for judgement, which is useful in emergencies but risky when the person in front of you does not fit.

Everyday picture: a satnav speaking at the junction changes the route; a map posted last week rarely does. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. When asked which strategy is most likely to change behaviour, choose the point-of-care, patient-specific reminder. When asked which is least likely, choose posting printed copies or other passive methods. Do not assume that different national recommendations mean one body appraised the evidence badly.

Exam trap: most and least likely to change behaviour, and why guidelines differ between countries. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Guyatt G, Rennie D, Meade MO, Cook DJ (2015). Users' Guides to the Medical Literature: Essentials of Evidence-Based Clinical Practice, 3rd ed. JAMA/McGraw-Hill.
  2. Straus SE, Glasziou P, Richardson WS, Haynes RB (2019). Evidence-Based Medicine: How to Practice and Teach EBM, 5th ed. Elsevier.

Open the full lesson in the course →

13.14.4Declarations of interest and funding

Big idea. Any interest that a reasonable reader might think could influence the work must be declared, including payments from companies that make competing products, because undeclared interests are hidden bias.
Picture it as a referee who mentions that his brother plays for one of the teams.

Syllabus: Declarations of interest and funding

Read more in your textbookEconomic Evaluation, QI & Governance, page 67 · Declarations of interest and research fraud →

The story in plain words. A referee whose brother plays for one team may be scrupulously fair, but the crowd deserves to know. Declaring an interest does not accuse anyone of bias; it lets the reader judge. The test is simple: could a reasonable reader think this might influence the work? Financial interests include fees, honoraria, consultancy, shares, grants and employment, and they include payments from the maker of a competing product, since that company gains if the reviewed drug looks worse. Non-financial interests include close relationships, advocacy roles and strongly held beliefs. ((? An author reviewing a dementia drug is paid to lecture by the maker of a rival drug. Must she declare it? ?)) Yes. It is a direct financial interest in the outcome of the review.

A simple test for what to declare. Financial and non-financial interests both count, including payments from makers of competing products. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. Lexchin, Bero, Djulbegovic and Clark showed in a 2003 systematic review that industry-sponsored studies were more likely to reach conclusions favourable to the sponsor. The International Committee of Medical Journal Editors requires a uniform disclosure form covering the previous 36 months, together with the role of the funder in design, analysis and the decision to publish.

From everyday life to the clinic. Ordinary clinical work, such as prescribing a class of drug or being paid by the NHS to see patients, is not a conflict in itself. Nor, usually, is a grant awarded to unrelated colleagues in the same institution. When appraising a paper, read the funding and declarations before the results, and ask who designed the trial and who held the data. Declaring is not the end of the matter. Editors and guideline bodies may ask a conflicted author to step back from a particular decision, and NICE committee members declare interests at every meeting.

Everyday picture: a referee announces that his brother plays for one team. Declaring is not an accusation; it lets the crowd judge. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The exam offers several honest-sounding options and one payment. Pick the payment from an interested company, including a competitor. A relative with the condition is a personal interest some journals ask about, but it is rarely the best answer when a financial interest is on the list.

Exam trap: pick the payment from an interested company, including a competitor. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Laupacis A, Sackett DL, Roberts RS (1988). An assessment of clinically useful measures of the consequences of treatment. New England Journal of Medicine, 318: 1728-1733.
  2. Moher D, Cook DJ, Eastwood S et al. (1999). Improving the quality of reports of meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials: the QUOROM statement. Lancet, 354: 1896-1900.

Try each one first. Then show the working and read the rule.

Challenge 1 · 13.9 EBM principles, evidence sources and guidelines · 13.1.2
The conventional hierarchy for treatment questions, tiers left blank. Illustrative material drawn for CDA.
The pyramid shown is the conventional hierarchy of evidence for questions about treatment effectiveness, with its tiers left blank. Which source of evidence belongs in tier 1, at the top?
  1. A large prospective cohort study
  2. A single large double-blind RCT
  3. A well-matched case-control study
  4. A consensus statement from an expert committee
  5. A systematic review and meta-analysis of high-quality RCTs
Show the working
Answer: E A systematic review and meta-analysis of high-quality RCTs

For questions about treatment, a systematic review and meta-analysis of well-conducted RCTs sits at the top: it reduces random error and lets consistency be judged.

A single large RCT is strong but below a review of several. Cohort and case-control studies are observational, and expert consensus is at the bottom.

Rule: Top = systematic review of RCTs.
Trap: Placing a single RCT above a systematic review of RCTs.
The top of the hierarchy for a treatment question. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: OCEBM Levels of Evidence Working Group (2011). The Oxford 2011 Levels of Evidence. Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine.

Challenge 2 · 13.9 EBM principles, evidence sources and guidelines · 13.1.2
Study types in random order beside a blank ladder. Illustrative material drawn for CDA.
The cards shown name six study types in random order. Which sequence correctly orders study types from strongest to weakest evidence for a treatment question?
  1. RCT, systematic review of RCTs, cohort, case-control, expert opinion
  2. Cohort, RCT, case-control, systematic review, case series
  3. Systematic review of RCTs, RCT, cohort, case-control, case series
  4. Expert opinion, RCT, cohort, case-control, case report
  5. Case-control, cohort, RCT, systematic review, expert opinion
Show the working
Answer: C Systematic review of RCTs, RCT, cohort, case-control, case series

The standard order for treatment questions is: systematic review of RCTs, single RCT, cohort, case-control, case series, then expert opinion.

Cohort studies rank above case-control studies because they follow exposure forward in time and are less prone to recall and selection bias.

Rule: SR of RCTs, RCT, cohort, case-control, case series, expert opinion.
Trap: Ranking cohort below case-control.
The standard order from strongest (1) to weakest (6) for treatment questions. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: OCEBM Levels of Evidence Working Group (2011). The Oxford 2011 Levels of Evidence. Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine.

Challenge 3 · 13.9 EBM principles, evidence sources and guidelines · 13.1.3
RowElementDecision in the draft plan
1DatabasesMEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO, from inception
2Citation chasingCheck reference lists of every included study
3ContactWrite to research groups known to work on body dysmorphic disorder
4Grey literatureExclude conference abstracts and unpublished theses
5LanguageInclude papers in any language; translate where needed
Draft search plan for a systematic review of psychological therapies for body dysmorphic disorder. Illustrative material drawn for CDA.
A team is planning a systematic review of psychological therapies for body dysmorphic disorder. Which search decision would most threaten the completeness of the review? The draft search plan is shown; each row is one decision.
  1. Searching MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO
  2. Checking the reference lists of included studies
  3. Writing to known researchers in the field
  4. Excluding conference abstracts and unpublished theses
  5. Including papers in languages other than English
Show the working
Answer: D Excluding conference abstracts and unpublished theses

A complete search uses several databases, chases reference lists, contacts experts and accepts any language.

Excluding conference abstracts and theses removes the grey literature, where negative studies often sit. Published studies show larger effects on average, so leaving the rest out biases the review towards benefit.

Rule: A complete search includes grey literature, experts and all languages.
Trap: Thinking non peer-reviewed material should always be excluded.
A complete search: four good practices ticked, the exclusion of grey literature crossed. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Hopewell S, McDonald S, Clarke M, Egger M (2007). Grey literature in meta-analyses of randomized trials of health care interventions. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MR000010.

Challenge 4 · 13.9 EBM principles, evidence sources and guidelines · 13.1.5
The trainee's notes. Illustrative material drawn for CDA.
A trainee wants to turn the question 'does exercise help my patients with depression?' into a structured, searchable clinical question. Which framework is designed for this? The trainee's notes are shown.
  1. PICO
  2. SWOT
  3. SMART
  4. SOAP
  5. SBAR
Show the working
Answer: A PICO

PICO splits the question into Patients, Intervention, Comparison and Outcome. Each part becomes a set of search terms, combined with AND.

SWOT, SMART, SOAP and SBAR are planning, goal-setting, note-taking and handover tools, not question frameworks.

Rule: Foreground treatment questions use PICO.
Trap: Confusing communication or documentation mnemonics with question frameworks.
The exercise question broken into PICO parts, each of which becomes a search concept. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Richardson WS, Wilson MC, Nishikawa J, Hayward RS (1995). The well-built clinical question: a key to evidence-based decisions. ACP Journal Club, 123: A12-13.

Challenge 5 · 13.9 EBM principles, evidence sources and guidelines · 13.1.7
ArmRelapsed within 12 months
Maintenance antidepressant60 / 200 (30%)
Placebo100 / 200 (50%)
Effect measure reportedValue (95% CI)
Odds ratio0.43 (0.28 to 0.65)
Relative risk reduction40% (23% to 53%)
p value (chi-squared)p < 0.001
Hazard ratio0.51 (0.37 to 0.71)

Results of a one-year maintenance trial in recurrent depression, as reported. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A patient with recurrent depression asks how much difference maintenance treatment would make to him. The results table from the main trial is shown. Which measure is most useful to explain the benefit to him?
  1. Odds ratio
  2. Relative risk reduction
  3. p value
  4. Hazard ratio
  5. Number needed to treat
Show the working
Answer: E Number needed to treat

In the table, relapse fell from 50% on placebo to 30% on maintenance: an absolute reduction of 20 percentage points, so the number needed to treat is 5 (95% CI 4 to 10). Treat five people like him for a year and one avoids a relapse he would otherwise have had.

Relative risk reduction, odds ratios and hazard ratios are relative measures that hide how common the outcome was. A p value says nothing about size. Give the NNT with its time frame and beside the number needed to harm.

Rule: Absolute measures (ARR, NNT) are best for informed decisions.
Trap: Quoting relative risk reduction alone, which inflates perceived benefit.
Icon array: relapse 50 in 100 without maintenance and 30 in 100 with it. Absolute risk reduction 0.20, number needed to treat 5. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Gigerenzer G, Gaissmaier W, Kurz-Milcke E et al. (2007). Helping doctors and patients make sense of health statistics. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 8: 53-96.

Challenge 6 · 13.9 EBM principles, evidence sources and guidelines · 13.12.1
Summary of the planned paper. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Authors are preparing a systematic review and meta-analysis of lithium for suicide prevention. Which reporting guideline should they follow? A summary of the planned paper is shown.
  1. CONSORT
  2. STARD
  3. STROBE
  4. SRQR
  5. PRISMA
Show the working
Answer: E PRISMA

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are reported with PRISMA (2009, updated 2020). It replaced QUOROM, the 1999 statement for meta-analyses of randomised trials.

CONSORT is for trials, STARD for diagnostic accuracy studies, STROBE for observational studies and SRQR for qualitative research.

Rule: Systematic review or meta-analysis: PRISMA.
Trap: Choosing QUOROM as if it were still current.
Study design decides the reporting statement. A systematic review or meta-analysis follows PRISMA. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Page MJ, McKenzie JE, Bossuyt PM et al. (2021). The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. BMJ, 372: n71.

Challenge 7 · 13.9 EBM principles, evidence sources and guidelines · 13.12.2
Excerpt from a second-round rating form; the panellist sees only the anonymous group summary. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A panel of experts rates draft statements anonymously over several rounds, seeing a summary of the group's ratings between rounds, until agreement is reached. An excerpt from a second-round rating form is shown. This is
  1. A focus group
  2. A cost-utility analysis
  3. A nominal group with open discussion
  4. The Delphi method
  5. A meta-regression
Show the working
Answer: D The Delphi method

The Delphi method gathers anonymous ratings from an expert panel over several rounds. After each round the group's summary is fed back, and panellists may revise their ratings.

Anonymity limits the pull of dominant voices; agreement is reached when the ratings converge. A focus group and a nominal group involve face-to-face discussion.

Rule: Delphi = anonymous iterative rounds to consensus.
Trap: Confusing Delphi with focus groups.
A Delphi panel of 12: anonymous ratings narrow over three rounds as the group summary is fed back. Grey bars show the interquartile range; the teal line is the median. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Hasson F, Keeney S, McKenna H (2000). Research guidelines for the Delphi survey technique. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 32: 1008-1015.

Baseline audit before the new guideline. Full monitoring means ECG, glucose, lipids and weight all recorded in the past 12 months. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A mental health trust wants clinicians to follow a new guideline on physical health monitoring for people on antipsychotics. Which strategy is most likely to change practice? The baseline audit is shown in the table.
  1. Emailing the guideline to all staff
  2. Presenting it once at a grand round
  3. Adding an automated, patient-specific prompt to the electronic record at each review
  4. Publishing it in the trust newsletter
  5. Asking a senior clinician to endorse it
Show the working
Answer: C Adding an automated, patient-specific prompt to the electronic record at each review

Prompts that reach the clinician at the moment of decision, about the patient in front of them, are among the most consistently effective ways to change practice, although the gains are modest.

Emails, newsletters, a single talk and senior endorsement are passive or one-off methods. They raise awareness but seldom change what clinicians do.

Rule: Point-of-care, patient-specific reminders beat passive dissemination.
Trap: Assuming awareness of a guideline is enough to change practice.
Implementation strategies from least to most likely to change practice. The order is conceptual. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Shojania KG, Jennings A, Mayhew A et al. (2009). The effects of on-screen, point of care computer reminders on processes and outcomes of care. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, CD001096.

Challenge 9 · 13.9 EBM principles, evidence sources and guidelines · 13.12.3

North team644164%

Baseline audit of lithium monitoring before the new guideline is rolled out. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A trust wishes to roll out a new national guideline on lithium monitoring. Which approach is LEAST likely to change clinicians' behaviour? The baseline audit is shown in the table.
  1. Electronic alerts when a patient's lithium level is overdue
  2. Educational outreach visits to each team
  3. Posting printed copies to every ward
  4. Audit with individual feedback to prescribers
  5. Involving local clinicians in adapting the guideline
Show the working
Answer: C Posting printed copies to every ward

Posting printed copies is passive dissemination: the least likely of these options to change behaviour.

Electronic alerts, educational outreach, audit with feedback and local adaptation are active strategies that reach clinicians where decisions are made, and they work better.

Rule: Passive dissemination is the weakest implementation strategy.
Trap: Thinking dissemination equals implementation.
Implementation strategies from least to most likely to change practice. Posting printed copies is the least. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Challenge 10 · 13.1, 13.2.4 Evidence, clinical questions and causation · 13.1.4
RecordWords in the titleTerm attached by indexers
1Major depression in later life: a primary care cohortDepressive Disorder, Major
2Unipolar depression and sleep: a randomised trialDepressive Disorder, Major
3Exercise for MDD: a pilot studyDepressive Disorder, Major
Illustrative records drawn for CDA.
The table shows three MEDLINE records whose authors describe the same condition in different words. A librarian advises adding the term in the right-hand column to the search so that all three are retrieved. What is this term?
  1. A truncation symbol
  2. A Boolean operator
  3. A Medical Subject Heading (MeSH)
  4. A free-text keyword
  5. A proximity operator
Show the working
Answer: C A Medical Subject Heading (MeSH)

MeSH headings are assigned by trained indexers, so one heading collects papers that describe the same concept in different words. Good strategies combine MeSH with free-text synonyms, because new papers may not yet be indexed. Embase uses Emtree; PsycINFO uses its own thesaurus.

In the table, three different title phrases map onto one indexing term: that is exactly what a MeSH heading does. Free text is added alongside it to catch papers not yet indexed.

Rule: Controlled vocabulary in MEDLINE: MeSH.
Trap: Relying on free text and missing papers that used a different term.

Source: Higgins JPT, Thomas J, Chandler J et al (eds) (2024). Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, version 6.5. Cochrane.

Challenge 11 · 13.1, 13.2.4 Evidence, clinical questions and causation · 13.1.4
#Search lineRecords
1psychosis.tw.14,862
2exercise.tw.21,407
31 AND 2164
.tw. = searched in title and abstract words.
Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
The search history shown returns 164 records, but checking the reference lists of key reviews shows that many relevant trials are missing. Which change will best broaden the search to capture them?
  1. Changing AND to NOT
  2. Adding 'AND randomised' to the string
  3. Restricting to English-language papers
  4. Combining synonyms with OR, for example 'exercise OR physical activity OR sport'
  5. Searching titles only
Show the working
Answer: D Combining synonyms with OR, for example 'exercise OR physical activity OR sport'

Within each concept, synonyms are joined with OR to capture all ways of describing it. Different concepts are then joined with AND, which keeps only records containing both. NOT should be used sparingly because it can exclude relevant papers.

Line 3 joins two single free-text words with AND. Exercise, physical activity and sport are synonyms for one concept, so join them with OR before combining with psychosis using AND. Another AND, a limit or a title-only search would shrink the 164 further.

Rule: OR broadens; AND narrows; NOT excludes.
Trap: Using AND between synonyms and losing relevant papers.

Source: Higgins JPT, Thomas J, Chandler J et al (eds) (2024). Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, version 6.5. Cochrane.

Challenge 12 · 13.1, 13.2.4 Evidence, clinical questions and causation · 13.1.1
Study summary
QuestionIs cannabis use linked to first-episode psychosis?
DesignCase-control
Cases200 people with first-episode psychosis from two early intervention services
Controls400 people without psychosis
ExposureCannabis use before the index date
Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A trainee is appraising the published study summarised in the table. Which is the single most important design-specific question to ask first?
  1. Were participants randomised with concealed allocation?
  2. Were cases and controls drawn from the same source population, with exposure measured the same way in both?
  3. Was the analysis by intention to treat?
  4. Was the funnel plot symmetrical?
  5. Was the sample size large enough to estimate prevalence?
Show the working
Answer: B Were cases and controls drawn from the same source population, with exposure measured the same way in both?

Critical appraisal starts with the design, because each design has characteristic weak points. For case-control studies these are how cases and controls were chosen and whether exposure was ascertained in the same way. Design-specific checklists such as CASP and the Newcastle-Ottawa scale make this explicit.

The summary does not say where the 400 controls came from or how cannabis use was measured in each group. Selection of cases and controls from the same source population, with exposure measured the same way, is the design-specific heart of case-control appraisal.

Rule: Appraise each design against its own key biases: case-control = selection and recall; cohort = attrition; trial = randomisation, concealment, blinding, ITT.
Trap: Applying trial criteria (randomisation, ITT) to an observational study.
Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Greenhalgh T (2019). How to Read a Paper: The Basics of Evidence-Based Healthcare, 6th ed. Wiley-Blackwell.

Challenge 13 · 13.1, 13.2.4 Evidence, clinical questions and causation · 13.1.7
GroupRelapsedStayed wellTotalRelapse at 1 year
Continued antidepressant4016020020%
Switched to placebo8012020040%
Total12028040030%
Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A woman with recurrent depression asks whether to continue her antidepressant. The table shows relapse over one year in a discontinuation trial. Which way of presenting this best supports an informed decision?
  1. 'Continuing halves your risk of relapse'
  2. 'The odds ratio for relapse is 0.38'
  3. 'Of 100 people like you, about 40 would relapse in a year without the tablet and about 20 with it'
  4. 'The result was statistically significant at p < 0.01'
  5. 'Most experts recommend continuing'
Show the working
Answer: C 'Of 100 people like you, about 40 would relapse in a year without the tablet and about 20 with it'

Working: 40% minus 20% is an absolute risk reduction of 20%, so the NNT is 5. The relative risk reduction is 50%, which sounds more impressive. Natural frequencies with a fixed denominator let people compare options without mental arithmetic.

From the table, relapse is 80 of 200 (40%) on placebo and 40 of 200 (20%) on continued treatment. The best answer turns these into natural frequencies with one denominator, 40 in 100 against 20 in 100, which shows a 20 in 100 difference and an NNT of 5 without arithmetic.

Rule: Use absolute risks as natural frequencies (x out of 100).
Trap: Quoting only the relative risk reduction.

Source: Gigerenzer G, Gaissmaier W, Kurz-Milcke E, Schwartz LM, Woloshin S (2007). Helping doctors and patients make sense of health statistics. Psychol Sci Public Interest, 8: 53-96.

Challenge 14 · 13.1, 13.2.4 Evidence, clinical questions and causation · 13.1.7
After explaining the benefits and side effects of lithium, a psychiatrist has the exchange shown with the patient. What is this technique?
  1. Motivational interviewing
  2. Teach-back
  3. Decision aid
  4. Framing
  5. Informed consent form
Show the working
Answer: B Teach-back

Teach-back puts the responsibility for clarity on the clinician: if the patient cannot explain it, the explanation was not good enough. It is recommended in shared decision-making guidance alongside decision aids and absolute risk presentation.

In the exchange the psychiatrist asks the patient to say, in their own words, what they would do. That is teach-back. It tests the clarity of the explanation, not the intelligence of the patient.

Rule: Patient explains it back: teach-back.
Trap: Asking 'Do you understand?' and accepting 'yes'.

Source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2021). Shared decision making. NICE guideline NG197.

Challenge 15 · 13.1, 13.2.4 Evidence, clinical questions and causation · 13.1.6
FeatureStudy X (experimental)Study Y (observational)
Research ethics approvalYesYes
Direction in timeProspective, 12 monthsProspective, 12 months
Matched on age and sexNoYes
Groups defined by exerciseYesYes
How people came to exerciseResearch team allocated them by computerPeople chose for themselves
Two studies of supervised exercise for depression. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
The table compares two prospective studies of supervised exercise for depression: Study X is experimental and Study Y is observational. What is the essential feature that distinguishes an experimental study from an observational one?
  1. It requires research ethics committee approval
  2. It is prospective
  3. Participants are matched on key confounders
  4. Groups are defined by their exposure
  5. The investigator assigns the exposure or intervention
Show the working
Answer: E The investigator assigns the exposure or intervention

In observational studies the researcher watches what happens to people exposed by choice or circumstance. Assigning the exposure, ideally at random, is what lets an experiment break the link between exposure and confounders.

In the table, both studies are approved, prospective and define groups by exercise, and only the observational one is matched. The defining difference is who decided the exposure: the research team in Study X, the participants themselves in Study Y.

Rule: Investigator allocates exposure = experimental.
Trap: Calling any prospective study experimental.

Source: Grimes DA, Schulz KF (2002). An overview of clinical research: the lay of the land. Lancet, 359: 57-61.

Challenge 16 · 13.1, 13.2.4 Evidence, clinical questions and causation · 13.2.4.1
Study PStudy Q
Who was recruited2,000 fifteen-year-olds, none with psychosis300 adults with psychosis and 600 without
When cannabis use was recordedAt age 15, at recruitmentAt interview, after diagnosis, asking about the teens
When psychosis was recordedAge 15 to 30, as it occurredAlready present at recruitment
Two studies of cannabis use and psychosis. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
The table summarises two studies of cannabis use and psychosis. For which Bradford Hill consideration does Study P give stronger evidence than Study Q?
  1. Temporality
  2. Analogy
  3. Biological plausibility
  4. Coherence
  5. Specificity
Show the working
Answer: A Temporality

Case-control studies measure exposure after the outcome, so recall and reverse causation can blur the time order. A cohort recruits people free of the outcome and records exposure first, establishing that the cause came first.

Study P is a prospective cohort that recorded cannabis use before psychosis appeared; Study Q is a case-control study that asked about the teens after diagnosis. Temporality is where the cohort wins, because recall and reverse causation can blur the order in Study Q.

Rule: Cohort shows exposure before outcome: temporality.
Trap: Assuming case-control studies give equally clear time order.

Source: Hill AB (1965). The environment and disease: association or causation? Proc R Soc Med, 58: 295-300.

Challenge 17 · 13.1, 13.2.4 Evidence, clinical questions and causation · 13.2.4.1
A local authority fits safety barriers to a bridge that was a frequent suicide site. The chart shows suicides at the bridge and at other local sites. Which Bradford Hill consideration does this best illustrate?
  1. Experiment
  2. Analogy
  3. Coherence
  4. Specificity
  5. Consistency
Show the working
Answer: A Experiment

Hill's experiment consideration includes natural or planned changes in exposure. Restricting access to lethal means, such as the detoxification of domestic gas in the UK, has repeatedly been followed by falls in suicide, supporting a causal role for method availability.

In the chart, bridge suicides fall from 50 in the six years before to 9 in the six years after, while other sites rise only from 21 to 27, so the total falls from 71 to 36. Removing the exposure and seeing the outcome fall is the experiment viewpoint in action; the detoxification of domestic gas in the UK is the classic national example.

Rule: Remove the exposure, outcome falls: experiment.
Trap: Calling any before-and-after change 'consistency'.
Site2012 to 20172018 to 2023Change
At the bridge509-41
Other local sites2127+6
All sites7136-35
Six years before and after the barriers, from the chart in the question.
The bridge fell by 41 while other sites rose by 6: at most partial displacement, so the total fell. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Kreitman N (1976). The coal gas story: United Kingdom suicide rates, 1960-71. Br J Prev Soc Med, 30: 86-93.

Challenge 18 · 13.1, 13.2.4 Evidence, clinical questions and causation · 13.2.4.3
Using Rothman's causal pie model, a researcher draws the two pies shown for psychosis. Pie 1 is made up of genetic liability, cannabis use and childhood adversity. What does complete pie 1 represent?
  1. A component cause
  2. A sufficient cause
  3. A necessary cause
  4. A confounder
  5. An effect modifier
Show the working
Answer: B A sufficient cause

Different people may develop the same disorder through different pies. Components in the same pie interact: none produces the outcome alone. This explains why most cannabis users never develop psychosis.

Genetic liability, cannabis and childhood adversity together complete pie 1, so the pie is a sufficient cause. Each single slice is only a component cause, and pie 2 shows that psychosis can arise through a different set of components.

Rule: Complete pie = sufficient cause; slice = component cause.
Trap: Calling a single slice sufficient.

Source: Rothman KJ (1976). Causes. Am J Epidemiol, 104: 587-592.

Challenge 19 · 13.1, 13.2.4 Evidence, clinical questions and causation · 13.1.2
Service question card
WhoAdolescents aged 13 to 18 seen for the first time with anorexia nervosa
What the service wants to knowHow many recover, relapse, stay unwell or die
Over what timeTen years from first presentation
Treatment being comparedNone: all receive usual care
The service has not yet chosen a design.
A service wants to know how adolescents with a first episode of anorexia nervosa fare. Its question card is shown. Which design gives the best evidence for this question?
  1. An inception cohort recruited at first presentation and followed up
  2. A randomised controlled trial of family therapy versus individual therapy
  3. A case-control study of adults with and without eating disorders
  4. A cross-sectional survey of current patients on a specialist unit
  5. A systematic review of qualitative interviews with recovered patients
Show the working
Answer: A An inception cohort recruited at first presentation and followed up

The best design depends on the question. Prognosis needs people assembled at the same early stage (an inception cohort) and followed with complete follow-up. Sampling people already in treatment favours those with persistent illness and gives a gloomier picture.

The card describes natural course over ten years with no treatment comparison: a prognosis question. The answer is a cohort assembled at first presentation. A trial answers a different question, and a clinic sample overweights the chronic cases.

Rule: Prognosis: inception cohort.
Trap: Assuming RCTs are always the top design whatever the question.
Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: OCEBM Levels of Evidence Working Group (2011). The Oxford 2011 Levels of Evidence. Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine.

Challenge 20 · 13.1, 13.2.4 Evidence, clinical questions and causation · 13.1.2
Users followed upExpected severe skin reactions
1,0000.1
10,0001
100,00010
500,00050
Expected reactions = users followed x 1/10,000.
Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A pharmacovigilance team suspects that a mood stabiliser is linked to a very rare, severe skin reaction, seen in roughly 1 in 10,000 users. The table shows how many reactions a cohort would be expected to see. Which design is most efficient for studying this harm?
  1. A randomised controlled trial powered for the skin reaction
  2. A cross-sectional survey of current users
  3. An ecological study comparing prescribing and reaction rates by region
  4. A single case report in a dermatology journal
  5. A case-control study comparing prior drug exposure in cases and controls
Show the working
Answer: E A case-control study comparing prior drug exposure in cases and controls

When the outcome is rare, a case-control study collects all available cases and compares their exposure with matched controls. A cohort would need to follow huge numbers to see enough events. If instead the exposure were rare and the outcome common, a cohort selected on exposure would be preferred.

The table shows that a cohort of 500,000 users would see only about 50 reactions. Starting with the cases and looking back at drug exposure is the efficient route.

Rule: Rare outcome (harm): case-control. Rare exposure: cohort.
Trap: Mixing up rare outcome (case-control) with rare exposure (cohort).

Source: Celentano DD, Szklo M (2019). Gordis Epidemiology, 6th ed. Elsevier.
